extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and readers considering the structure and ratification of a federal union (readers of The Federalist; politically engaged public circa 1787 and modern readers of constitutional theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria and historical lessons for judging the strengths and weaknesses of confederacies and federal unions, drawn from ancient and modern examples (Greece, Achaean league, Germanic empire, Netherlands, Swiss cantons, Poland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of power in particular depositories
rubrics_metrics.description: The CONCENTRATION of large portions of the strength of the community into particular DEPOSITORIES (either in individuals or political bodies) is a defining feature shared by feudal baronies and separate governments in a confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton/Madison argue this concentration produces rivalry and challenges to central authority; it parallels feudal baronies where large depositories of strength enabled sustained opposition to sovereign power. Example: comparison of feudal baronies and U.S. state governments. Antipattern: allowing unchecked aggregation of local military/economic power without national counterbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments' confidence can oppose national authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate governments in a confederacy 'will generally possess the confidence and good-will of the people, and with so important a support, will be able effectually to oppose all encroachments of the national government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This local legitimacy can enable states to resist necessary national measures. The authors treat popular confidence in local governments as a double-edged sword: good for local governance but dangerous when it permits obstruction of legitimate federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence (national allegiance) of federal deputies
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal powers administered by deputies 'appointed wholly by the cities in their political capacities' are weak because those deputies act as agents of their states rather than of the federal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amphictyonic council example: deputies appointed by cities resulted in corruption and domination by powerful members (Athens, Sparta, Thebes). Guidance: federal representatives should not be mere state agents if a functioning national authority is required; antipattern is purely state-controlled federal delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and enforceability of federal sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal system must have a SANCTION to its laws; without an effective sanction, federal laws are 'wanting' and unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that the 'total want of a SANCTION to its laws' is a palpable defect of the Confederation. Amphictyons theoretically had coercive authority but enforcement failed in practice. Scoring note: presence of legally-backed, practicable means to enforce federal decrees is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of laws, weights, measures, and money
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the member cities/states 'had all the same laws and customs, the same weights and measures, and the same money' the federal system functioned with more moderation and less disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achaean league example: uniformity promoted moderation/justice and tempered popular turbulence. Practical guidance: common legal and economic standards support cohesive federal action and reduce interstate friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty-over-sovereigns is a structural vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities' (as opposed to individuals) is 'a solecism in theory' and 'subversive of the order and ends of civil polity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that federal laws addressed to sovereign communities rather than individuals make the federal body nerveless and ineffective. Recommendation: federal authority must be able to operate on individuals/subjects, not only on states as collective sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-rule design: unanimity undermines action
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements of unanimity (as in the United Netherlands) render federal decision-making impracticable and prevent collection of contributions or timely treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: States-General often required unanimity and could not levy contributions or act swiftly; constitutional practice was frequently waived. Guidance: avoid unanimity rules for core federal functions; adopt decision rules that enable timely national action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central executive or 'spring' to coordinate action (with attendant risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A central figure (e.g., the Dutch stadtholder) or powerful member can act as a 'spring' within the union to quicken action and prevent dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a central executive can supply the force to overcome anarchy (examples: stadtholder, Holland's dominance), it also concentrates power and risks tyranny. Balance needed: an executive capable of enforcing union without degenerating into despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and efficiency in military preparation and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal bodies must be able to prepare and field national military forces without being delayed by 'tedious discussions' and the jealousies of sovereign members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germanic empire example: slow diet deliberations left armies unready and enemies in the field. Criterion: ability of federal decision-making to meet exigencies promptly is essential to self-defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common fiscal, military, monetary, and judicial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a common treasury, common troops, common coin, and a common judicatory are markers of a functioning union; their absence (as among the Swiss cantons) weakens the confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swiss example: no common treasury, troops, coin, or judicatory — kept together by geography and necessity rather than institutional strength. Guidance: robust common institutions are needed for stability; otherwise union depends on temporary expedients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks against domination by the most powerful members
rubrics_metrics.description: A confederacy must prevent its most powerful members from 'tyranniz[ing] successively over all the rest' (Athens, Sparta, Thebes examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic patterns show powerful members often dominate councils and corrupt deputies of weaker members. Federal design should include mechanisms to check dominant states and protect weaker members' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to foreign influence and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A confederacy must guard against foreign powers exploiting internal divisions (Philip of Macedon, Roman manipulation, neighboring powers' intrigues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Philip entered councils by intrigue and bribes; Rome seduced members from leagues. Criterion: internal unity and institutional resilience reduce vulnerability to external interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to maintain internal order and dispense justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal system must be capable of maintaining public order and dispensing justice among its members; failure to do so produces 'general imbecility, confusion, and misery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germanic empire and circle system experiments show that failed enforcement and justice mechanisms lead to devastation or ineffective remedies. Practical guidance: federal institutions must include reliable enforcement and impartial adjudication mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lawful magistracy rather than military violence to enforce order
rubrics_metrics.description: A good federal system substitutes 'the mild and salutary COERCION of the MAGISTRACY' for the 'destructive COERCION of the SWORD'—i.e., legal authority should replace brute force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The closing moral: lawful, institutional coercion is preferred to ad hoc military enforcement. Antipattern: reliance on arms and violence to compel compliance rather than established legal processes.
